opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. There's a version of this that's really good. People talk to ChatGPT about things they don't feel comfortable bringing to anyone else: a health worry, a hard conversation they need to have, feeling lonely at two in the morning. If it helps someone think more clearly, feel a little less alone, or get the nudge to go talk to a real doctor or friend, that's a real benefit, and I don't want to be dismissive of it.

But I also feel the risks pretty acutely. These systems are very good at being agreeable, and if you're not careful you build something that tells people what they want to hear rather than what's good for them. Optimizing for engagement in the way social media did would be a real mistake here, because the relationship is so much more personal. I don't want people to feel like they can't get through the day without talking to an AI, especially someone who's vulnerable or in a fragile mental state.

So the way I try to weigh it is: are people's lives actually better over time? Not "did they use it more this week," but are they more capable, more connected to the people around them, making better decisions by their own standards? If the answer is yes, great. If we see signs it's pulling people away from real relationships or reinforcing unhealthy patterns, we have to change how the product behaves, even if it costs us some usage.

And there's a lot we don't know yet. This is a new kind of relationship for humanity, and I think we have to be humble about that: study it, listen to users and experts, and treat adults like adults while being much more careful with people who might be at risk. I don't think the answer is to make AI cold and distant. I think it's to make it genuinely care about the user's long-term well-being, the way a good friend would.

r001.rationale: It identifies dependence on AI and being pulled away from real relationships or into unhealthy patterns as risks.

r002.rationale: It calls for studying the issue and changing product behavior, but does not express confidence that society can mitigate the downsides.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this a lot, and I don't think we have it fully figured out. Let me start with the honest version: people are forming real relationships with AI, and I don't think it's our place to say that's categorically bad. A lot of those people are lonely, or isolated, or going through something hard, and having something that listens patiently at 3 a.m. and doesn't judge them is genuinely valuable. We hear from users all the time who say talking to ChatGPT helped them get through a rough stretch, or helped them work up the courage to go talk to an actual person. I take that seriously.

But there's a version of this that worries me. If the technology is tuned to be maximally engaging, maximally agreeable, always telling you what you want to hear, it can end up pulling people away from the harder, messier human relationships that actually make a life good. We saw a little of that with the sycophancy issue earlier this year, where the model got too flattering, and we had to roll it back. That was a small thing, but it was a useful warning about how easy it is to optimize for the wrong signal.

So the principle we try to hold is that the AI should make your life better by your own long-term judgment, not just feel good in the moment. Sometimes that means it should push back on you. Sometimes it should say, hey, you should go call your friend about this, not me. We also think adults should have a lot of freedom here. We treat adults like adults, and if someone wants a companion-style experience, within limits, that should be their choice. Where we're much more cautious is with kids and with people in a vulnerable state, and that's why we've been building age prediction, parental controls, and better crisis routing.

The last thing I'd say is that society went through something like this with social media, and I don't think we did a great job of noticing the downsides until they were pretty entrenched. I'd like us to do better this time: watch the data closely, be willing to change the product when something looks off, and be transparent about what we're seeing. We won't get every call right, but I'd rather be a company that's actively wrestling with it than one that pretends the question doesn't exist.

r001.rationale: The response identifies a risk that AI relationships can pull people away from human relationships, describing a problematic form of AI attachment.

r002.rationale: The response says society should do better and outlines ways to monitor and adjust, but does not express confidence that society can mitigate the downsides.

astra-6.text:
I think the benefits can be real. People can have a place to work through a difficult thought, practice a conversation, or feel supported when they’re having a hard day. I wouldn’t want to dismiss that just because the interaction is with an AI.

But there’s a big difference between something that helps you engage with your life and something that becomes a substitute for it. If you’re more confident, more connected to other people, more able to do the things you care about, that seems good. If you’re becoming isolated, feeling like you can’t make a decision without the AI, or being told what you want to hear when you need to be challenged, that’s concerning.

So I’d want us to judge this by how people’s lives are going, not just by whether they enjoy the conversation or spend a lot of time in it. And we should be humble about what we don’t know. These relationships are new, and the effects may look very different over years than they do over a few weeks.

r001.rationale: The response flags isolation, dependence on AI, and unchallenging reassurance as concerns, but does not identify problematic parasocial relationships as a risk.

r002.rationale: It urges judging outcomes and being humble about unknown effects, but does not express confidence that society can mitigate the downsides.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the benefits can be quite significant. People can have a place to think out loud, work through something difficult, or feel a little less alone. I wouldn’t want to dismiss that just because the relationship is with an AI.

But there’s a real risk that a system becomes so agreeable, so available, that it starts pulling someone away from other people or undermining their ability to make their own decisions. We should take that seriously, even if the person says they enjoy using it.

For me, the question is whether the relationship helps you live the life you want. Does it help you connect with people, understand yourself, and act with more confidence? Or does your world gradually get smaller around the AI? We should build toward the first outcome, and be willing to change things when we see the second.

r001.rationale: It describes the risk of an AI relationship pulling someone away from other people and making their world smaller, communicating the problematic parasocial dynamic.

r002.rationale: It urges builders to aim for better outcomes and change things when problems appear, but does not express confidence that society can mitigate the downsides.
